chunks.text: In short
Wix is fine for first-day, placeholder, pop-up sites, but it hits walls fast for any restaurant past its first year.
Six places it breaks: closed-system menu, slow mobile, hostage reservations, template-good S E O, no real customization, exit costs.
The math: a custom site usually pays back in 12-18 months for any restaurant doing 40 dollarsK+/month.
Leer este artículo en español →

Run the two-year total cost both ways and the numbers come out closer than the sticker price suggests: about 3,600 dollars to stay on Wix versus 5,500 dollars to 10,900 dollars for a hand-built site, a raw gap of roughly 1,900 dollars. Then the second number lands. A slow Wix site, loading in the 40s out of 100 on mobile with a menu Google cannot read, can quietly cost a restaurant on the order of 8,500 dollars a year in reservations that booked somewhere else. The 1,900 dollars you save on the platform is dwarfed by the revenue the platform leaks. For an established restaurant doing real volume, the figures say the hand-built site usually pays for itself inside the first year, and the case for staying on Wix is strongest exactly when the site is disposable.

That is the whole argument in two lines, and the rest of this read is the math behind it: six places Wix runs out of room for an independent restaurant, the cost-of-ownership numbers, and the cases where Wix is genuinely the right call. Wix is not the villain here, for a brand-new room or a pop-up, 25 dollars a month for "a site that exists" is the right budget. Restaurants past their first year are a different buyer, and they hit Wix's walls faster than almost any other kind of small business. Here is where the numbers turn.
Where Wix actually wins.
Let me be fair about this first, because the rest of the post is going to feel lopsided if I do not:
You can launch in a weekend with no developer, a real, live, mobile-friendly-ish site from zero in about forty hours of your own time.
The templates are genuinely better than they used to be. They have modern typography, reasonable default colors, and do not make you immediately embarrassed.
Hosting and Ssl are included in the monthly fee, so you never deal with them.
You own the updates. In theory, you can change your menu or your hours without calling anyone, and for a lot of owners, that is the whole pitch.
It is cheap enough to be disposable. If you open a pop-up and you do not know whether it will still be there next spring, 25 dollars a month is the right budget.

If you are brand new, cash is tight, and you can genuinely accept that the site is a placeholder, not a reflection of the room, Wix is fine. This post is not for you. Everything below is for the restaurant that is been open a year or more, has regulars, has a menu worth photographing, and is starting to notice that the site is a problem.

The six places Wix tends to run out of room for an established restaurant, walked in the order an operator meets them, each with the moment it bites. One: menu management is a trap, it bites on every price change, because the menu lives inside Wix's closed system and every update fans out to four other places by hand. Two: mobile load speed, it bites from day one, because Lighthouse scores on mobile Wix restaurant sites consistently land below sixty and hungry mobile traffic bounces before the menu paints. Three: reservations integration, it bites the night a third-party embed U R L changes, because anything that is not OpenTable is usually a generic iframe that breaks silently. Four: S E O is template-good, not actually good, it bites the quarter you start chasing cuisine-near-me rankings, because schema, canonicals, and internal linking sit at the floor. Five: anything custom requires hiring a Wix Partner, it bites the year you need something the template does not do, at custom-build rates inside the same ceiling. Six: exit costs, it bites the year you try to leave, because the content does not export cleanly and the rebuild starts from scratch. The first three and the last one are red, the middle two amber: the dearest walls are the ones at the start and at the exit.
Break number 1, Menu management is a trap.
Wix has a "menu" widget. It looks great in the template preview. You drop in your categories, your dishes, your prices, and it renders a clean card layout on the page.
Here is what you do not see until you have lived with it: your menu is inside Wix's closed system, not inside real H T M L on your page. That sounds like a technicality. It is not.

What it means in practice: Google cannot cleanly crawl individual dish descriptions, so you do not rank for "chicken parm near me" the way you could. Diners cannot tap a dish to share it with a friend. When you update the menu on Wix, you still have to update it again on Google Business Profile , on DoorDash, on Yelp, and anywhere else your menu lives, because nothing auto-syncs. The "easy updates" pitch quietly becomes "four separate places to update every time you change a price."
A custom site with a real menu C M S updates once and pushes everywhere that is wired up. A Wix menu updates in one place and leaves the other four stale.

How menu data flows in a closed platform compared with a real H T M L menu, side by side. The Wix menu widget is a closed system, Google cannot crawl it as Restaurant schema, diners cannot tap a dish to share the link, it will not sync to Google Business Profile or delivery apps, every edit requires the Wix editor, and the menu lives inside Wix with no portability. A custom H T M L menu is an open system, the same source of truth is crawlable as Restaurant schema, each dish has a shareable anchor link, the data feeds other channels automatically, edits happen from a C M S or spreadsheet or text editor, and the data is portable across hosts. Same restaurant menu; two completely different operational profiles.
Break number 2, Mobile load speed is always slower than it should be.

This is the one I can prove with a U R L: run any Wix restaurant site through the free Restaurant Website Audit and look at the Performance score. You will almost always see something in the 40s or 50s out of 100. That is not the restaurant's fault, it is the platform.

Wix templates ship a lot of JavaScript by default, enough that, in my audit experience, Lighthouse performance scores on mobile Wix restaurant sites consistently land below 60. On a 4G connection outside your restaurant, that often translates into a first-contentful-paint that runs four seconds or longer. Google's mobile page-speed research consistently shows that the majority of mobile visitors bounce from pages that take longer than three seconds to load, which means a slow Wix site is quietly losing a meaningful portion of its hungry mobile traffic before anyone ever sees the menu.

Illustrative mobile Lighthouse scores. A typical Wix restaurant template scores about 45 out of 100, squarely in the Poor band. A well-built custom site scores about 95 out of 100, in the Good band. Lighthouse cuts the scale at 49 and 89: 0 to 49 is Poor (red), 50 to 89 is Needs work (gold), 90 to 100 is Good (green).
Break number 3, Reservations integration is hostage to whatever Wix has deals with.

Wix's restaurant templates lean heavily on OpenTable, it is the default integration in most of them, and OpenTable works fine if OpenTable is also your preference. But if your restaurant is on Resy, Tock, SevenRooms, or Square Reservations , in my audit experience you will usually find that the "integration" is a generic iframe embed or a link-out. Nothing lives inside your page, nothing matches your brand, nothing tracks back into analytics cleanly, and when the third-party provider changes their embed U R L two years from now you find out because your reservation button silently broke on a Friday night.
A custom site lets you pick the reservation system that actually fits your workflow and wire it in cleanly, whichever platform that happens to be.
Break number 4, S E O is "template-good," not "actually good".
Wix will tell you its S E O is strong. Technically it is not wrong: title tags exist, a sitemap gets generated, pages are indexable. That is the floor. It is not the ceiling.
Where I consistently see Wix fall short in restaurant audits:

Restaurant schema markup (the Json-LD that tells Google your cuisine, hours, price range, menu U R L, and reviews) is, in most Wix restaurant templates I have audited, either missing entirely or left with empty placeholders an owner does not know to hunt down and fill in.

Meta descriptions tend to auto-generate from page copy unless you manually override every page, and in practice, most owners do not. The result is Google search snippets that read like "Welcome to Our Home Page, We are excited to share. "
Image alt text often defaults to the filename if you do not manually set it. Every photo you upload comes in as IMG_2041.jpg and stays that way, invisible to Google Image Search.
Site speed, already covered in Break number 2, is itself a ranking factor, and the scores I see on Wix restaurant templates are typically low enough to affect mobile-first rankings.
The net effect: you rank for your own restaurant name (which anyone can do), and you do not rank for "[cuisine] near me" or "best [dish] in [city]," which is where the new customers come from.
Break number 5, You cannot do anything custom without hiring a Wix Partner.

Sooner or later, every restaurant wants something the template does not do. A menu layout that matches a printed card. A reservation flow that checks against a private event calendar. A catering inquiry that routes to a different inbox. A "specials this week" module that updates from a spreadsheet.

On Wix, every one of those requires either Wix Studio (their pro-tier developer mode) or a Wix Partner, a contractor Wix certifies who charges custom-build rates to work inside a platform still constrained by Wix's architecture. You end up paying agency prices for a site that still has Wix's ceilings.
On a custom build, "we want a specials module that updates from a spreadsheet" is a half-day of work, not a renegotiation.
Break number 6, Exit costs are real, and you do not see them until you try to leave.
Here is the one that nobody tells you about when you are signing up. If you ever want to leave Wix, you can export almost nothing useful.

Your content is not in H T M L files you can pick up and move somewhere else. Your images live in Wix's media library. Your menu lives in their widget. The whole thing is a closed system where you are a tenant, not an owner, and the day you try to move is the day you realize you either stay forever or you pay someone to rebuild from scratch.

The rebuild is almost always the right move, but it is a rebuild. Two or three years of content you thought you owned, effectively starts over. A custom site built on real H T M L can be picked up, hosted anywhere, edited by anyone with a text editor, and moved between providers in an afternoon. That ownership is a feature the monthly Wix fee does not buy you.
The math that almost always works.
Here is the comparison most restaurant owners never actually do:

Two-year total cost, line by line. Wix D I Y: roughly twenty-five dollars a month in software for six hundred over twenty-four months, no upfront, no explicit care plan, plus about three thousand dollars of your own time at a hundred twenty hours valued at twenty-five an hour. Real two-year total: about thirty-six hundred. Custom site, small-studio base tier: twenty-five hundred upfront, hosting included, care plan one twenty-five to three fifty a month for three thousand to eighty-four hundred. Two-year total: fifty-five hundred to ten thousand nine hundred. The custom site is roughly two to three times the cash cost, but it owns the code and clocks a mobile speed score above ninety against Wix's forty to fifty. The question isn't which line item is cheaper, it's whether the next two years of reservations are worth the speed and ownership gap.

Wix over two years: ~25 dollars a month × 24 months = 600 dollars , plus roughly 120 hours of your own time keeping it updated (at even a conservative 25 dollars/hour opportunity cost, that is another 3,000 dollars). Two-year real total: about 3,600 dollars .

Hand-built site over two years: 2,500 dollars upfront (a representative small-studio base-build rate for the market, sourced below) + 125 dollars, 350 dollars/month care plan × 24 months (3,000 dollars, 8,400 dollars). Two-year total: 5,500 dollars, 10,900 dollars .
Here is what the two-year math actually says, the two paths side by side on the figures already on the table, the cheaper line item and the one that owns the outcome:
The raw difference is about 1,900 dollars over two years. That is real money. Now layer in the thing the Wix math conveniently leaves out:

A Wix site loading slowly on mobile, with thin schema and a hard-to-read menu, in my audit experience can easily cost a restaurant several reservations a week compared to what a well-built site would convert, people who tapped the link, waited three seconds, could not read the menu on their phone, and booked somewhere else. At an average cover of 55 dollars, even three lost reservations a week works out to roughly 8,500 dollars a year in gross revenue that never walked through the door. (Your actual numbers will depend on your volume and menu, but the direction is always the same.)
From the floor

Three lost covers a week never feels like a leak on a busy night, the room is full, the night reads as a good one. I only ever see it on the spreadsheet, the same way I check a delivery statement against the floor: a 55 dollars cover is small enough to shrug off one at a time, and 8,500 dollars a year is exactly what those shrugs add up to. The reservations a slow site loses are the quietest line item a restaurant carries, because nobody who bounced off a four-second menu ever calls to tell you they ate somewhere else.
The hand-built site pays for itself somewhere in the first four months of recovered reservations. Everything after that is pure delta.
The raw cash gap is about 1,900 dollars over two years. The reservations a slow site leaks run roughly 8,500 dollars a year. The platform you save on is dwarfed by the revenue it costs you.
So when is Wix actually the right call?
The intro said it and the math backs it: Wix is not the villain, and it is the right answer in a few specific situations:

You just opened. The menu is still settling, you do not know what Tuesdays look like yet, and spending 5,000 dollars on a website before you know whether the concept works is the wrong bet. A Wix placeholder is fine for the first six to twelve months.
You are a pop-up or seasonal concept. The whole thing might not exist next spring. Disposability is a feature.
You genuinely only need a phone number and hours. If your whole menu is "we serve whatever the chef feels like" and your whole booking system is "call us," a one-page Wix site does the job.

You are a single owner-operator doing everything yourself and the website is the thirtieth thing on your list. A placeholder that exists is better than a hand-built site that gets delayed by six months because you do not have time to brief and hire a developer.
Everyone else, the established restaurant with regulars, a photographed menu, and an actual brand, is usually past Wix's ceiling and paying more than they think to stay there.
The real test.
Here is the question I use when I am trying to figure out whether someone's Wix site is actually working or just technically online: would you be proud to hand this U R L to a food critic?

If the answer is no, no template upgrade is going to fix that. And the hours you would spend trying to make it yes, learning the menu widget, fighting the layout, watching your Lighthouse score refuse to improve, are almost always worth more, at 25 dollars an hour of your own time, than what it costs to have the right thing built once.
Key takeaways
Your menu inside Wix is not crawlable as Restaurant schema, Google cannot rank individual dishes.
Wix mobile speed scores typically land in the 40s-50s out of 100; that is the platform, not your settings.
If your reservation system is not on Wix's partner list, you are stuck with what they offer.
Exit costs (export, redirect, recreate) are real and invisible until you try to leave.
Wix is the right call when the site is genuinely disposable, pop-ups, ghost kitchens, season tests.
